newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU ends talks united on trade, at odds on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: EU ends talks united on trade, at odds on Iraq.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers united on Sunday in condemning Washington's trade sanctions against Cuba, Libya and Iran but were at odds in weekend talks over U.S. bombing raids on Iraq.

They bristled at U.S. legislation which could punish some European firms for operating in any nation on Washington's trade hit list but said they were unlikely to take retaliatory steps until after the U.S. presidential elections in November.

Ministers from the 15-nation bloc condemned Saddam Hussein's incursion into Kurdish areas of northern Iraq last week, calling on him to pull back his troops, but failed to send Washington the kind of backing it gave after Iraq's 1990 Kuwait invasion.
"We secured a significant measure of agreement on the situation in Iraq," host Dick Spring, the Irish foreign minister, told a news conference at the end of the talks.

But Irish officials acknowledged that the failure to back the Clinton administration's bombing of Iraq reflected a divergence of views which ranged from France's lukewarm response to Britain's enthusiastic support.

They also backed the reinstatement of an agreement allowing Iraq to sell limited amounts of oil to buy food and medicine as soon as the United Nations secretary-general, who suspended the agreement, judges it right to do so.
Spring held out the possibility that the EU might remain involved in Bosnia, which brought the horrors of war to the EU's doorstep, for another two years after elections this year.
He said there was a need for a continued "civilian and military" presence during a two-year consolidation period after the elections and the end of the NATO peace force's mandate in December.

"Everything so far has been easy compared with what lies ahead," said Carl Bildt, the international community's representative for Bosnia, who briefed EU ministers on the reconstruction of the country on Saturday.
The EU appeared to back down from a confrontation with Israel over its plans to send a fact-finding trio of ministers for talks with the PLO in its Orient House offices in disputed East Jerusalem.

Spring said on Saturday that the so-called troika of ministers from Ireland, Netherlands and Italy wanted to go to Orient House, a move that would infuriate the Israeli government which sees Jerusalem as its unified capital.

But the EU is now checking whether the PLO itself wants to meet in East Jerusalem after a visit to Dublin last week by Israeli Foreign MInister David Levy, who told Spring PLO chairman Yasser Arafat had agreed to move the office elsewhere.

EU states, worried that the momentum of the Middle East peace process might be lost with the election of the right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, called on him to revive the peace talks and carry out its commitments.

Spring said their hopes for peace were raised by talks last week between Arafat and Netanyahu but the meeting urged the Israeli government to leave the city of Hebron, as the peace agreement stipulates, and to allow free movement of people.

The ministers set October 5 as the date for an extra summit the Dublin government has been asked to hold to review the progress of talks by a standing inter-governmental conference (IGC) to discuss a revision of the EU's founding treaties.
The review is supposed to be finished by the middle of next year to streamline the EU for the 21st century and an influx of countries from eastern Europe.
